title: Monoids: Identity, Uniqueness and the Standard Examples
quickIdea: A monoid is a semigroup that owns an identity element. It is the exact home of string concatenation and the classic 'monoid but not a group' answer in GATE.
remember: A monoid is a set with an associative binary operation and a two-sided identity e: a e = e a = a for every a in the set.
The identity of a monoid is unique: if e and e' both fix everything then e = e e' = e'.
(Sigma*, concatenation) is the standard monoid: closed, associative, identity is the empty string, and no non-empty string has an inverse, so it is not a group. GATE CSE 1996 Q.2.4 asks exactly this.
(N0, +) with 0 included is an abelian monoid; without 0 the same set is only a semigroup. (Z, x) is an abelian monoid with identity 1 that is not a group, because 2 has no inverse in Z.
(2^X, union) is an abelian monoid with identity the empty set; (2^X, intersection) is an abelian monoid with identity X. Neither is a group when X is non-empty.
(Z, max) is a semigroup and not a monoid: max(m, e) = m for every integer m would need an e below every integer, and Z has no least element. GATE CSE 1997 Q.3.1 is this question.
A monoid in which every element cancels is a group when the monoid is finite, but not in general: (N0, +) cancels and is not a group.

example.prompt: Take Sigma = {a} and the set Sigma* of all finite strings over it. Which rungs does (Sigma*, concatenation) reach?
example.work: Closure: concatenating two finite strings gives a finite string. Associativity: (uv)w and u(vw) are both the string u followed by v followed by w. Identity: the empty string eps satisfies eps u = u eps = u. Inverses: if a v = eps then the length equation 1 + |v| = 0 has no solution, so a has no inverse.
example.answer: An abelian monoid that is not a group; every non-empty string fails the inverse axiom.

gateAngle: GATE gives a monoid and asks whether it is a group. After closure, associativity and identity, the only live question is whether each element has an inverse inside the set, and the answer usually turns on the set being cut short: N, Sigma*, Z under multiplication, matrices with integer entries.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Is (2^X, union) a group?
variations.answer: No. It is an abelian monoid: the identity is the empty set, and A union B = empty forces both A and B empty, so only the empty set has an inverse.
variations.why: Commutativity and identity are easy to confirm and people stop there. The inverse axiom is the one that fails.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: How many elements of (Z_10, x) have a multiplicative inverse?
variations.answer: Four: the units 1, 3, 7 and 9, counted by phi(10) = 4.
variations.why: The units of Z_n form the group U(n) of size phi(n); the rest of Z_10 is only a monoid, which is why the count is not 10.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: On the integers define a star b = min(a, b). Which rung does (Z, star) reach?
variations.answer: A commutative semigroup only. An identity would have to be at least as large as every element, and Z has no largest element. On a finite set {1, ..., n} the same operation is a monoid with identity n.
variations.why: The same formula lands on different rungs depending on the set, so the set is part of the question, not background.

trap.what: Taking the empty set as the identity for intersection, or 0 as the identity for max.
trap.why: The identity must fix every element, not merely look neutral: A intersection empty = empty, which is not A, and max(0, -5) = 0, which is not -5.
trap.counterexample: In (2^X, intersection) with X = {1, 2} the identity is X, since A intersection X = A; the empty set fails because {1} intersection empty = empty.

check.question: Is (Z, x) a monoid, and is it a group?
check.answer: An abelian monoid, not a group: the identity is 1, but 2 has no multiplicative inverse in Z.
check.explanation: Multiplication of integers is closed and associative, and 1 fixes every integer, so the monoid rung is reached. The inverse of 2 would have to satisfy 2b = 1, and no integer b does, so the inverse axiom fails for every element other than 1 and -1.
